steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three days when Elias began to hear the sea speaking in its place.

He noticed it on a Tuesday, just after dawn. The world beyond the glass was a gray, shifting wall; waves shouldered each other in sullen ranks, and gulls pinwheeled in the mist like lost scraps of paper. The horn was broken—some wiring deep in the belly of the tower had corroded—and the repair boat would not come until the storm season passed. Until then, it was just him, the lamp, and the sea.

He kept to his routines. Routines were railings you could hold when sleep blurred the edges of day.

At six, he wound the clockwork that turned the lens. At seven, he checked the kerosene reserves, though the lamp had been electric for years. At eight, he circled the catwalk, watching the thin white pulse of the light stride out into the gray. Ships passed rarely now; radar and satellites did most of the work his tower had once done. Still, the light swept on, stubborn and precise, as if unaware that the world had moved past it.

The first voice came just after noon.

Elias was halfway down the iron stair, one hand on the rail, when a sound rose through the stones: a soft, deliberate knocking, not wind, not wave. He stopped. The tower vibrated faintly with each strike, like a tuning fork touched by an unseen hand.

He listened. Three knocks. A pause. Two knocks. Another pause. Three again.

Morse, he thought, without meaning to. Old memory rolled over him in a slow, reluctant wave. He had learned the code forty years ago, when they still trained keepers for all eventualities.

S… E…

He waited, breath held. Nothing more. The silence that followed was so complete it seemed to weigh on his shoulders.

“Sea,” he muttered, annoyed with himself, and continued down.

But the pattern returned the next day. And the next.

Always when the tide turned. Always that same shivering through the stones, that same hesitating code: three, one, three. S E A.

He did not tell anyone. There was no one to tell. The radio sat on his desk like a sleeping animal, silent unless he reached out and pressed its throat. The repair crew checked in every few days, their voices scratchy with distance; he told them the light was fine, the tower was sound, the storm was easing. All of that was true.

He did not mention that the ocean had learned to knock.

Instead, he answered.

On the fourth day, when the pattern came again, he stood on the lowest landing with a rusted wrench in his hand. Ridiculous, he thought, but his fingers were already moving. He struck the rail: one sharp clang, then three, then one.

E L I

The sound ran up the spiral of the stairs and out through the tower like a thrown stone. He felt foolish, suddenly, like a man talking to a mirror. But the foolishness eased something tight in his chest.

Above him, the lamp continued its patient rotation, casting its beam over an empty sea.

Knock. Knock. Knock.

S. E. A.

He answered each time the tide turned. Three times a day, every day. Soon the pattern widened: not just the word, but letters strung together, uncertain and slow. He kept an old notebook by the stair and wrote them down, listening as if eavesdropping on a conversation in the next room.

H E L P, it said, on the seventh day.

“Who?” he asked aloud, before he remembered that he was speaking to an ocean.

He walked the narrow ring of the catwalk, scanning the horizon. Nothing moved but the gray. No flares. No cries. No shapes in the water but the heaving, hurrying waves.

The next message took three tides to complete.

D O W N

“Down where?” he asked.

The sea did not answer in words. It simply climbed, tide by whispering tide, gnawing at the rocks that rooted the tower. The spray reached higher on the stones; the gusts of salt through the open hatch tasted colder. He dreamed of ropes, of hands slipping from them, of lights sinking until the dark folded over them like a book.

On the radio, the repair crew talked of schedules and budgets and the long list of things that broke faster than they could be fixed. No one mentioned the foghorn. No ships had been lost. No names had been read on the weather channel.

Perhaps, Elias thought, the sea was speaking of something older than ships.

He began to answer with more than his name. When the tower trembled with that patient code, he tapped the rail until his fingers stung.

W H O

Silence, and then, slowly:

B O A T

He could picture it. The current here was treacherous, curling around the submerged teeth of rock. He had seen small fishing boats dragged sideways, engines straining, before the light caught their wheelhouse windows and warned them off.

“When?” he whispered.

The reply came in one long, halting spill of knocks that blurred together. He wrote them down as he heard them, tracing their rhythm like the edge of a scar.

Y E A R S

Elias leaned his forehead against the cool iron of the stair. A long-ago wreck, then. No record he’d read, no flare he’d seen. Storms could swallow a boat here as quietly as a stone dropped down a well.

He slept badly that night. When he closed his eyes, he saw a hull overturned on the black chalk of the seabed, barnacles claiming its flanks, fish moving through its open ribs. Faces, blurred by water and time, watched the slow pulse of the distant, unreachable light.

The next day, the sea’s message changed.

C O L D, it said. D A R K.

And, after a longer pause:

A L O N E.

Elias did not write those words down. He could feel them without ink: in the creak of the tower during high wind, in the echoing hollowness that spread out in all directions when he stepped outside at midnight, the beam whirling over waves that swallowed it without comment.

He had become a keeper young and stayed, while the others took jobs in town, ran marinas, sold their small houses on the cliff. When automation came and budgets shrank, he had not fought to be transferred. “Someone has to mind the light,” he’d told the inspector, but it was not really about the ships. It was about this stone room, this faithful mechanism, this narrow space between sea and sky where he could listen to something larger than himself breathe.

Now something else was listening back.

That afternoon, he carried a small wooden crate up to the lantern room. It had been meant as a shelf for spare bulbs, but he set it carefully on the outer ledge, inside the rail, and anchored it against the wind. Inside he placed an old brass compass, its glass clouded but its needle still eager, and a coil of cotton rope. Gifts of a sort, he thought, for a ship that would never dock.

He did not know if the sea could see them, or care.

When the tide turned, the knock came again.

H E R E

His hands shook as he answered.

S E E Y O U

There was a long pause. Then, in tiny, hesitant taps, like a child’s hand on a door:

L I G H T

He looked at the lamp. Its beam cut through the fog in precise increments, white and tireless. Far below, the waves flashed as the light swept them, each crest limned for an instant in silver.

“Yes,” he said aloud. “I’m here.”

He stayed awake through the night for the first time in years, pacing the catwalk, watching the dark. Once, just before dawn, he thought he saw something move below: not a ship, not a wave, but a pale hint of shape, circling slowly among the rocks. A reflection, he told himself. A trick of the eyes. The cold climbed his ankles anyway, like water soaking cloth.

When the repair boat finally came a week later, the sky had cleared. The men climbed the steps with boxes and tools, stamping salt from their boots, filling the tower with the rough comfort of other voices. Elias made coffee. He listened to them swear at rusted bolts and laugh about a new deckhand’s seasickness. None of them mentioned the way the stones seemed to hum underfoot.

“You been all right out here, Elias?” the youngest asked, wiping grease from his fingers.

“Fine,” Elias said.

“Lonely, I mean.”

He considered. The lens turned. The light swept. Somewhere under the waves, wood softened. Iron bloomed with salt.

“Not as much as you’d think,” he answered.

They fixed the horn in the afternoon. When they tested it, the sound burst from the cliff with brutal, living force, rolling out over the water, bouncing back in long, staggering echoes. It drowned the smaller sounds: the wind at the window, the slap of wave on stone, the delicate, familiar knock that had begun to live between the tower’s heartbeats.

That night, the fog horn bellowed steadily at its appointed intervals. The sea struck the rocks in time with it, heavy and impersonal. When the tide turned, the tower did not shiver with code.

The silence was different now. Thicker. Deliberate.

Elias sat halfway down the stairs, hands on his knees, listening for a sound that did not come. After an hour, he picked up the wrench and tapped the rail anyway, his blows lost in the horn’s breath.

E L I

The metal rang. The sea continued its ruined applause against the cliff.

He waited through one tide, then another. Nothing. The notebook lay open beside him, its latest page half-filled with unfinished sentences of dots and dashes, a conversation abandoned mid-thought.

On the third tide, near dawn, when the fog horn paused between calls, something almost too faint to hear brushed up through the stone: a single, exhausted knock.

O N

He held his breath so tightly his chest hurt. The horn roared. He nearly missed the second syllable, a wavering tap squeezed into the sliver of quiet.

W A Y

A laugh broke out of him, dry and startled, like a cupboard opening after years of being stuck. He scrambled to his feet, grabbed the rail.

“Good,” he said, though there was no need to say it aloud. He struck the iron in slow, careful rhythm, timing his knocks in the narrow hush between the horn’s breaths.

I W I L L K E E P T H E L I G H T O N

The answer came, not in letters this time, but in a different language—the heavy, deliberate drag of the tide easing back, the gentler slap of wave on rock. The storm season had broken. The sea was going elsewhere.

So was whatever had borrowed its voice.

Years later, when the automatic systems finally replaced him and the tower’s door was locked, people in the town would talk about how the light still worked even when the power cut out, and how, on certain misty mornings, the sea seemed to knock at the cliff in patient patterns, as if counting, or spelling, or remembering.

By then, Elias would be living in a small room above the harbor, the beam of the lighthouse a thin pale stroke on his wall at night. Sometimes, when the fog rolled in and the horns from the big ships moaned across the bay, he would tap the wooden arm of his chair with his fingers: short, long, short, the old code etched into his hands.

From his window, the lighthouse looked like a single unwavering star. He watched it until the beam found him, just for a second, and imagined the flash sliding on, over the dark water, down into the places where wrecks slept and old conversations waited.

He tapped once more, the slightest of knocks on the sill.

Here, he told the sea, and whatever else was listening. Still here.
